where_to_find: The world's only wild red wolves live on the Albemarle Peninsula around Alligator River and Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuges; the Red Wolf Center's howling programs near Columbia are the best way to hear them.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park and the Blue Ridge Parkway, and on the coast at Alligator River and Pocosin Lakes refuges, where big bears walk farm fields at dusk.
fun_fact: Eastern North Carolina grows some of the biggest black bears anywhere; males over 800 pounds have been recorded on the coastal plain.
spotting_tip: Scan fields and road edges at dusk, and stay at least 50 yards away.
safety_note: Never approach or feed a bear; approaching within 50 yards is illegal in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Back away slowly if one comes toward you.

where_to_find: Cataloochee Valley in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, and the fields beside the Oconaluftee Visitor Center near Cherokee.
fun_fact: Elk vanished from North Carolina by the late 1700s; 52 were brought back to Cataloochee Valley in 2001–2002, and the herd has grown to about 200.
spotting_tip: Watch the valley fields early or late in the day, and stay 50 yards away, especially during the fall rut.
safety_note: Approaching within 50 yards is illegal in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Bulls charge in fall and cows guard calves in spring.

where_to_find: Everywhere; try William B. Umstead State Park, Blue Ridge Parkway meadows, or any greenway at dusk.
Statewide but secretive; quiet dawn walks at Umstead State Park or Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge give the best chance.
spotting_tip: Scan field edges and trailsides slowly at dawn; bobcats often sit still watching for rabbits and rodents.

fun_fact: Coyotes only reached North Carolina in the 1980s and now live in all 100 counties.

fun_fact: In North Carolina's Sandhills, fox squirrels are often jet black with a white nose and ears, and they're much rarer than gray squirrels.
spotting_tip: Walk open longleaf pine forest and look on the ground under the pines; they're about twice the size of a gray squirrel.
